+# Informationally complete pairs and forests
+
+## Abstract
+
+Two finite real random variables determine every probability weight exactly when their joint value map is injective and their bipartite fiber graph is a forest.
+
+**Definition 1.1 (The distribution on an arbitrary set).**
+
+$$\forall (\alpha: \operatorname{Type}*), ([\operatorname{Fintype}\left(\alpha\right)] [\operatorname{DecidableEq}\left(\alpha\right)], (\forall (f: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), (\forall (\mu: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), (\forall (\delta: \operatorname{Set}\left(\mathbb{R}\right)), ((\operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.distribution}\left(f, \mu, \delta\right): \mathbb{R}) = \operatorname{Finset.sum}\left(\operatorname{Finset.filter}\left(\lambda (x: \alpha) \mapsto (f\left(x\right) \in \delta), (\operatorname{Finset.univ}: \operatorname{Finset}\left(\alpha\right))\right), \lambda (x: \alpha) \mapsto (\mu\left(x\right))\right))))))$$
+
+*Formalization.* `D5/S3/Observer/Tomography/InformationallyCompletePairForest.distribution` (`✓ std3`).
+
+*Citation.* Stan Gudder (2019). *Finite-Dimensional Convex Effect Algebras*. DOI: [10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110). URL: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05110v1>.
+
+*Commentary.*
+
+For a real random variable f on a finite type α and a real weight μ, the value of the distribution on δ is the sum of μ over the points whose f-values lie in δ. This is the distribution in Section 5, lines 435–439 of the TeX source, extended to arbitrary real weights and arbitrary finite types. No measurability restriction is needed on δ because the sum is finite.
+
+**Definition 1.2 (Informational completeness of a pair).**
+
+$$\forall (\alpha: \operatorname{Type}*), ([\operatorname{Fintype}\left(\alpha\right)] [\operatorname{DecidableEq}\left(\alpha\right)], (\forall (f: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), (\forall (g: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), ((\operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.IsICPair}\left(f, g\right)) \Leftrightarrow (\forall (\mu: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), (\forall (\nu: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), ((\operatorname{D5.S3.TotalVariation.CycleSingleCutMinimax.Probability}\left(\mu\right)) \to ((\operatorname{D5.S3.TotalVariation.CycleSingleCutMinimax.Probability}\left(\nu\right)) \to ((\operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.distribution}\left(f, \mu\right) = \operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.distribution}\left(f, \nu\right)) \to ((\operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.distribution}\left(g, \mu\right) = \operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.distribution}\left(g, \nu\right)) \to (\mu = \nu)))))))))))$$
+
+*Formalization.* `D5/S3/Observer/Tomography/InformationallyCompletePairForest.IsICPair` (`✓ std3`).
+
+*Citation.* Stan Gudder (2019). *Finite-Dimensional Convex Effect Algebras*. DOI: [10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110). URL: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05110v1>.
+
+*Commentary.*
+
+The pair f, g is informationally complete if equality of both distributions forces equality of the probability weights μ and ν. Probability means that every weight is nonnegative and the sum of the weights is one. Equality of distributions is equality as functions on all subsets of the real line. This is the definition at line 474 of Section 5 of the TeX source; the finite type α may also be empty or have a single element.
+
+**Definition 1.3 (The bipartite fiber graph).**
+
+$$\forall (\alpha: \operatorname{Type}*), ([\operatorname{Fintype}\left(\alpha\right)] [\operatorname{DecidableEq}\left(\alpha\right)], (\forall (f: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), (\forall (g: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), ((\operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.fiberGraph}\left(f, g\right): \operatorname{SimpleGraph}\left(\operatorname{Sum}\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}\right)\right)) = \operatorname{SimpleGraph.fromRel}\left(\lambda (v: \operatorname{Sum}\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}\right)) \mapsto (\lambda (w: \operatorname{Sum}\left(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}\right)) \mapsto (\operatorname{Sum.elim}\left(\lambda (a: \mathbb{R}) \mapsto (\operatorname{Sum.elim}\left(\operatorname{Function.const}\left(\mathbb{R}, \operatorname{False}\right), \lambda (b: \mathbb{R}) \mapsto (\exists (x: \alpha), ((f\left(x\right) = a) \land (g\left(x\right) = b))), w\right)), \operatorname{Function.const}\left(\mathbb{R}, \operatorname{False}\right), v\right)))\right)))))$$
+
+*Formalization.* `D5/S3/Observer/Tomography/InformationallyCompletePairForest.fiberGraph` (`✓ std3`).
+
+*Source.* Repository-derived.
+
+*Acknowledgement.* Stan Gudder (2019). *Finite-Dimensional Convex Effect Algebras*. DOI: [10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110). URL: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05110v1>.
+
+*Commentary.*
+
+The vertices are two tagged copies of the real line. A left vertex a and a right vertex b are adjacent exactly when some x has f(x) = a and g(x) = b. SimpleGraph.fromRel makes this relation symmetric and excludes loops. There are no edges within either tagged copy, and values outside the ranges of f and g are isolated vertices. Several points with the same joint value give the same simple edge; injectivity of the joint value map records the absence of that multiplicity.
+
+**Theorem 1.4 (The forest characterization).**
+
+$$\forall (\alpha: \operatorname{Type}*), ([\operatorname{Fintype}\left(\alpha\right)] [\operatorname{DecidableEq}\left(\alpha\right)], (\forall (f: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), (\forall (g: \alpha \to \mathbb{R}), ((\operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.IsICPair}\left(f, g\right)) \Leftrightarrow ((\operatorname{Function.Injective}\left(\lambda (x: \alpha) \mapsto ((f\left(x\right), g\left(x\right)))\right)) \land (\operatorname{SimpleGraph.IsAcyclic}\left(\operatorname{D5.S3.Observer.Tomography.InformationallyCompletePairForest.fiberGraph}\left(f, g\right)\right)))))))$$
+
+*Proof.* Machine-checked in Lean as `D5/S3/Observer/Tomography/InformationallyCompletePairForest.result` (`✓ std3`). ∎
+
+*Resolves.* `Problems/gudder-2019-informationally-complete-pairs` (proved) by `D5/S3/Observer/Tomography/InformationallyCompletePairForest.result`.

+*Acknowledgement.* Stan Gudder (2019). *Finite-Dimensional Convex Effect Algebras*. DOI: [10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1912.05110). URL: <https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05110v1>.
+
+*Commentary.*
+
+The joint value map is injective exactly when every nonempty intersection of an f-level set and a g-level set is a singleton. This is complementarity in Section 5, lines 507–508 of the TeX source. The equivalence characterizes the IC pairs asked for at line 588: complementarity must be accompanied by acyclicity of the fiber graph. It holds for every finite α, including the empty and singleton cases.
+
+First, two distributions for f are equal if and only if the weights have equal sums on every f-level set. Evaluating the distributions on singletons proves necessity. For sufficiency, group the finite sum over the inverse image of any δ by the finitely many f-values occurring there, and apply equality on each level set.
+
+If the joint value map is not injective, take distinct points x and y with both f(x) = f(y) and g(x) = g(y). The point masses at x and y are distinct probabilities, but each random variable has the same distribution under the two point masses. Thus an IC pair has an injective joint value map.
+
+Assume the joint value map is injective. A trail p from u to v in the fiber graph determines a signed weight w on α. Its f-level sum at a is the indicator of u = Sum.inl(a) minus the indicator of v = Sum.inl(a); its g-level sum at b is the indicator of v = Sum.inr(b) minus the indicator of u = Sum.inr(b). Moreover, w is nonzero exactly at the points whose edges occur in p, and every absolute weight is at most one. To construct w, start with the zero weight on the empty trail. Prepending an edge from left to right adds the point mass with coefficient one at its unique point; prepending an edge from right to left adds the point mass with coefficient minus one. The trail condition keeps that edge out of the tail, so its previous weight is zero. Injectivity identifies its point uniquely, preserving the support description and the absolute bound. The marginal sums telescope to the stated endpoint indicators.
+
+Any nonzero w with absolute weights at most one and zero sums on all f-level sets and g-level sets gives distinct probabilities with equal distributions. Indeed, a nonzero coordinate makes α nonempty. Let n be its cardinality cast from a natural number to a real number, so n is positive. Summing the f-level sums gives total weight zero. Put μ(x) = (1 + w(x))/n and ν(x) = 1/n. The absolute bound makes μ nonnegative, and both total weights are one. The zero level sums make the two distributions agree for f and for g, while a nonzero coordinate of w makes μ and ν distinct.
+
+A cycle is a nonempty closed trail. Its endpoint indicators cancel, so the signed trail weight has zero sums on every level set. Some edge occurs in the cycle, and the exact support description makes this weight nonzero. The preceding perturbation then contradicts informational completeness. Combining this with injectivity proves that every IC pair has an acyclic fiber graph.
+
+Conversely, suppose the joint value map is injective and the fiber graph is acyclic. Let probabilities μ and ν have equal distributions for f and for g. For w = μ − ν, every f-level sum and every g-level sum is zero. Suppose w is nonzero, and retain only the edges arising from points where w is nonzero; call this graph H. It is a subgraph of the fiber graph and hence acyclic. Its edge set is contained in the image of finite α, so H has finitely many edges and is locally finite. A nonzero coordinate supplies an edge of H. Its connected component C contains both tagged endpoints, and is therefore a nontrivial tree with finitely many edges. Such a tree has vertices of degree one; choose one of them, u, with its unique neighbor q.
+
+The edge from u to q comes from a point y with w(y) nonzero. If u is a left vertex a, every other point z in the f-level set at a has weight zero: a nonzero weight would give another neighbor of u in C, so uniqueness of q forces g(z) = g(y), and injectivity then forces z = y. Thus the f-level sum is w(y), contradicting its vanishing. If u is a right vertex, the identical argument uses its g-level set and forces equality of the f-values. Both possibilities contradict w(y) being nonzero. Consequently w = 0, so μ = ν and the pair is IC.
+

+# Informationally complete pairs and forests

+/-- The distribution of a real random variable, evaluated on an arbitrary set. -/
+def distribution {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
+    (f : α → ℝ) (μ : α → ℝ) (δ : Set ℝ) : ℝ :=
+  ∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun x => f x ∈ δ), μ x
+
+/-- The two marginal distributions determine every probability weight uniquely. -/
+def IsICPair {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (f g : α → ℝ) : Prop :=
+  ∀ μ ν, Probability μ → Probability ν →
+    distribution f μ = distribution f ν → distribution g μ = distribution g ν → μ = ν

+/-- A point supplies an edge between its two tagged random-variable values. -/

+    Sum.elim (fun a => Sum.elim (fun _ => False)
+      (fun b => ∃ x, f x = a ∧ g x = b) w) (fun _ => False) v)

+private def supportGraph {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]

+private lemma distribution_eq_iff_fiber_sums {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
+    (f : α → ℝ) (μ ν : α → ℝ) :

+      ∀ a, (∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun x => f x = a), μ x) =
+        ∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun x => f x = a), ν x := by

+  constructor
+  · intro h a
+    have ha := congrFun h ({a} : Set ℝ)

+        ∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun x => f x = a), μ x := by
+      unfold distribution
+      simp only [Set.mem_singleton_iff]
+    have hν : distribution f ν ({a} : Set ℝ) =

+      unfold distribution
+      simp only [Set.mem_singleton_iff]

+      intro x hx

+          ∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun x => f x = a), q x := by

+        apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+        intro a ha

+private lemma zero_fibers_not_ic {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]

+# Informationally complete pairs are exactly complementary pairs with forest fiber graphs
+
+## Problem
+
+S. Gudder, *Finite-Dimensional Convex Effect Algebras* (2019), arXiv:1912.05110v1, Section 5, ends with this question. The following is the verbatim TeX text at line 588 of `finitedimensionalCEA.tex` (md5 `9dfe03bd484881c9db3b8b737095b005`):
+
+> We conclude from Example~5 that complementarity is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for IC. It is an open problem to find a simple characterization of IC for a pair $\brac{f,g}\subseteq\rscript (X)$.
+
+The source macros denote $\{f,g\}$ and $\mathcal R(X)$, respectively. Here $X=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge2$, $\mathcal R(X)$ consists of all maps $X\to\mathbb R$, and a probability weight $\mu$ has $\mu(x)\ge0$ and $\sum_x\mu(x)=1$. Its distribution under $f$ is $\Phi_{f,\mu}(\Delta)=\sum_{x:\,f(x)\in\Delta}\mu(x)$ for every $\Delta\subseteq\mathbb R$ (TeX lines 435–439). The pair is informationally complete (IC) when, for every two probability weights $\mu,\nu$, equality of their distributions under both $f$ and $g$ implies $\mu=\nu$ (line 474).
+
+Let $\Gamma(f,g)$ have vertices in two tagged copies of $\mathbb R$, with a left value $a$ adjacent to a right value $b$ exactly when some $x\in X$ satisfies $f(x)=a$ and $g(x)=b$. Issue [#23501](https://github.com/the-omega-institute/trureturing/issues/23501) fixes the reading:
+
+$\{f,g\}$ is IC if and only if $x\mapsto(f(x),g(x))$ is injective and $\Gamma(f,g)$ is acyclic.
+
+Injectivity is precisely the source's complementarity condition: every nonempty intersection of an $f$-level set and a $g$-level set is a singleton (lines 507–508). The characterization is proved, for every finite domain, without the restriction $n\ge2$. The definitions and source locators are also recorded in [the literature note](../Library/Observer/gudder2019finiteconvexeffect.md).
+
+## Motivation
+
+Gudder (2019), arXiv:1912.05110v1, Section 5, line 433, asks about pairs of individually incomplete observables:
+
+> For example, we would like to characterize pairs of observables $(A_1,A_2)$ that are informationally complete where $A_1$ and $A_2$ are not.
+
+The section reduces the sharp classical setting to random variables on a finite probability space. Its Theorem 5.2 gives strong complementarity as a sufficient condition and complementarity as a necessary condition; neither converse is asserted. The forest condition fills the gap between these two conditions using only the two level-set partitions. It determines when separate marginal distributions identify every underlying probability weight, including weights with zero coordinates.
+
+## Gap
+
+The bounded literature check recorded in #23501 reports:

+- the v1 source explicitly leaves this characterization open; the arXiv record lists only v1 and no journal reference;

+## Route
+
+All the module's lemmas below concern a finite type $\alpha$ with `Fintype α` and `DecidableEq α`, and real-valued maps $f,g:\alpha\to\mathbb R$.
+
+1. **Replace distributions by level sums.** `distribution_eq_iff_fiber_sums`, for any real weights $\mu,\nu$ and any $f$ on this finite domain, equates equality of distributions on all subsets of $\mathbb R$ with equality of the sums on every $f$-level set. No probability hypothesis is needed for this lemma. Singleton sets give one direction; finite grouping by values gives the other.
+2. **Exclude repeated joint values.** `not_injective_not_ic` assumes that $x\mapsto(f(x),g(x))$ is not injective. Distinct points with the same joint value give distinct point-mass probabilities with equal distributions under each map. Thus `ic_injective`, assuming `IsICPair f g`, obtains injectivity.
+3. **Construct signed trail weights.** `walk_weights` assumes joint injectivity and a walk $p$ from $u$ to $v$ in `fiberGraph f g` satisfying `p.IsTrail`. It constructs $w:\alpha\to\mathbb R$ with $|w(x)|\le1$, nonzero exactly at the points whose edges occur in $p$. Its $f$-level sum at $a$ is $\mathbf{1}_{u=\operatorname{inl}(a)}-\mathbf{1}_{v=\operatorname{inl}(a)}$; its $g$-level sum at $b$ is $\mathbf{1}_{v=\operatorname{inr}(b)}-\mathbf{1}_{u=\operatorname{inr}(b)}$. The signs depend on the direction in which an edge crosses the bipartition.
+4. **Turn a cycle into indistinguishable probabilities.** `zero_fibers_not_ic` assumes a nonzero real weight $w$, the bound $|w(x)|\le1$ at every point, and zero sums on every $f$-level set and every $g$-level set. Nonzeroness implies $n=|\alpha|>0$; the lemma constructs the distinct probability weights $\mu(x)=(1+w(x))/n$ and $\nu(x)=1/n$ with equal distributions. `cycle_not_ic` assumes joint injectivity and that `fiberGraph f g` is not acyclic. A cycle is a nonempty closed trail, so `walk_weights` gives a nonzero weight whose endpoint contributions cancel, satisfying all the hypotheses of `zero_fibers_not_ic`. Hence an IC pair with an injective joint map has an acyclic graph, as stated in `ic_acyclic`.
+5. **Use a leaf in the nonzero support.** `injective_acyclic_ic` assumes joint injectivity and acyclicity of `fiberGraph f g`. Given probability weights $\mu,\nu$ with equal distributions under both maps, put $w=\mu-\nu$. Every level sum is zero. If $w\ne0$, `supportGraph f g w` is an acyclic subgraph with finitely many edges, by `supportGraph_edge_finite`. A component containing an edge from a nonzero coordinate is a nontrivial tree; it has finitely many edges and is locally finite. These are the hypotheses of `SimpleGraph.IsTree.exists_ne_and_degree_eq_one`, which supplies a degree-one vertex. Joint injectivity makes its level sum equal to the single nonzero weight on its incident edge, a contradiction. This leaf argument is applied to that nontrivial component, not to isolated vertices of the ambient graph. Therefore $\mu=\nu$.
+
+`result` combines these directions into the stated equivalence.

+## Falsifier
+
+The settlement would not answer the source's question if informational completeness or the graph encoded different data. The module uses:
+
+- probability weights with every coordinate nonnegative and total mass one, via `CycleSingleCutMinimax.Probability`;
+- distributions as functions on every subset of $\mathbb R$, not just expectations or a joint distribution;
+- two tagged copies of the real line, so equal real numbers occurring as an $f$-value and a $g$-value remain different vertices;
+- a simple fiber graph, which merges repeated joint values, together with an explicit injectivity condition that detects this multiplicity.
+
+The real vertex set need not be finite: its edge set is finite, and values outside the ranges are isolated. The empty domain has no probability weight of total mass one, so its IC condition is vacuous; its joint map is injective and its graph has no edges. On a singleton domain there is one probability weight, an injective joint map, and one edge. Both cases are included in `result`.

+### What the settlement shows
+
+**Proved by `result`:** for every finite type $\alpha$ with decidable equality and every $f,g:\alpha\to\mathbb R$, equality of the two distributions determines every probability weight uniquely if and only if the joint value map is injective and the bipartite fiber graph is acyclic.
+
+**Computed, not formalized** (codex-cli, exact enumeration): across all pairs of set partitions on labelled domains of zero through six points, no disagreement was observed between full column rank of the stacked block-incidence matrix and the conjunction of joint injectivity and acyclicity of the simple bipartite graph.
+
+**Argued, not formalized.**
+
+- *Why the rank comparison tests the same information.* For a nonempty finite domain, the stacked block-incidence matrix sends a real weight to its two lists of level sums. Full column rank makes equal marginal lists imply equal weights. Conversely, a nonzero kernel vector has total sum zero, by summing the $f$-block equations. Scale it to have absolute coordinates at most one; perturbing the uniform probability as in `zero_fibers_not_ic`, with the nonzero, bounded, zero-level-sum hypotheses all satisfied, gives distinct probabilities with the same marginal lists. Thus the obstruction concerns identification of probability weights as well as signed weights. The empty-domain matrix has no columns and no kernel obstruction.
+- *Both conditions are sharp.* With two points and both maps constant, the graph is a single edge but the joint map is not injective; the two point masses are indistinguishable, as in `not_injective_not_ic`. Gudder's Example 5 has $P(f)=\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}$ and $P(g)=\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}$ (TeX lines 563–586). Here the joint map is injective and the graph is a four-cycle, meeting both hypotheses of `cycle_not_ic`. Adding $\varepsilon(1,-1,-1,1)$ to the uniform probability, with $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$, preserves all four block masses and gives a distinct probability. Complementarity alone therefore leaves an alternating cycle ambiguity.
+- *The source's sufficient condition is stronger than necessary.* Strong complementarity means every point is a singleton block for at least one map (TeX lines 528–533). It implies joint injectivity, since a singleton block cannot contain a second point with the same joint value. Every edge of its graph has a degree-one endpoint, which excludes cycles. A three-edge path is a forest even though its middle edge has neither endpoint of degree one. For instance, take $f=(0,0,1)$ and $g=(0,1,1)$: both maps repeat a value, but the $g$-block at $0$ determines the first mass and the $f$-block at $1$ determines the third; total mass determines the second. This gives an IC pair outside strong complementarity and outside individual injectivity, matching the form of the second pair in the source's Example 3.
+- *Relabelling extends the criterion.* For maps from a finite domain into arbitrary value sets, restrict to their finite images and injectively label each image by real numbers. This preserves every level set and identifies the active bipartite graphs, hence preserves both marginal information and cycles. Applying `result` to the relabelled maps gives the corresponding criterion; a compiled theorem for arbitrary codomains is not supplied here.
